outcome: The general statement — that the assembly map is an isomorphism — remains open in the coefficient-free form and was already known false in general with coefficients before the frozen revision (Higson–Lafforgue–Skandalis, 2002). No result since 26 January 2024 changes the status of the statement as given; all activity found is either progress on special group classes (cases, not the general problem) or work on a related permanence-property question.
summary: I searched broadly for any development on the Baum–Connes conjecture (the general statement that the assembly map is an isomorphism) since 26 January 2024, and found nothing that changes the status of the problem as stated. Wikipedia's own current article confirms the conjecture (without coefficients) 'is still open,' and that the version with coefficients was already refuted before the frozen revision via the Higson–Lafforgue–Skandalis counterexample (2002) — so nothing in the window bears on that either. The activity I found in the window consists entirely of case-restricted or related-problem work, none of which touches the general bullet: (1) Ellis, Rodríguez Cirone & Tartaglia, arXiv:2502.19111 (26 Feb 2025) — an expository writeup of the already-known proof of Baum-Connes for the infinite dihedral group D∞, following Higson–Kasparov; not a new result and, being an old case, would at most be `partial`/`open_stale` for that sub-case, not a change to the general problem. (2) A 'localization algebra approach to the Baum-Connes conjecture for extensions' (arXiv:2506.18446, ~June 2025) and (3) 'The Baum-Connes conjecture for extensions' by Ralf Meyer, arXiv:2508.05726 (submitted 7 Aug 2025, revised 29 Aug 2025) — the latter is a 2-page note giving a counterexample showing that Chabert–Echterhoff's permanence-property hypotheses for group extensions cannot be simplified; this is a negative result about a technical simplification of a proof technique, not about the Baum–Connes assembly map itself, and does not touch the general conjecture's truth value. (4) A December 2025 preprint on strong bolicity and Baum-Connes for relatively hyperbolic groups (arXiv:2512.21169) and an L^p/coarse Baum-Connes line of papers (2411.15070, 2311.05333) — all restrict to specific classes of groups or spaces (coarse geometry variants), which are cases or variants, not the stated problem. None of these results change what a careful reader would write in the bullet 'the assembly map is an isomorphism': that remains open in general and false with coefficients, exactly as before 26 January 2024. I found no AI involvement anywhere in this literature — all located papers are traditional human-authored pure-mathematics arguments, and a targeted search for any AI-assisted or Lean-formalization work touching Baum-Connes specifically returned nothing relevant.
competing_reading: One could argue the D∞ exposition (arXiv:2502.19111) or the relatively-hyperbolic-groups paper (arXiv:2512.21169) should be logged as `partial` progress on a case of the conjecture, since settling Baum-Connes for a specific group class does restrict territory from the general statement per §3.1's case-vs-variant test. I did not take this reading because (a) the D∞ result is explicitly an exposition of a pre-existing, decades-old proof (not new since 2024), and (b) results for specific group classes are a routine, continuous stream that predates the window by decades and does not represent a change in what is known about the conjecture's *general* truth value — the conjecture's own Wikipedia status line has not moved. If the strong-bolicity relatively-hyperbolic-groups result is judged genuinely novel and in-scope, the correct code would be `partial` / `progress` with `ai_role` still `none`, since no AI is credited in any of these papers regardless of classification.
what_would_settle_it: A published announcement, preprint, or expert digestion that either (a) proves or disproves the coefficient-free Baum-Connes assembly-map isomorphism for a substantial new class of groups not previously known, explicitly framed as new progress on the general conjecture (rather than an exposition or a permanence-technique note), or (b) any credible claim — refuted or standing — of a general resolution. No such source was found.
